idea: Replace random selection with a target-similarity filter plus dedup. Steps: (1) Fit a TfidfVectorizer on char n-grams (analyzer='char_wb', ngram_range=(1,3), sublinear_tf=True, max_features=50000) using the first 2000 chars of each pool doc and target_sample doc. (2) Train a LogisticRegression (C=1.0, max_iter=200) with positives = the 200 target_sample docs (class_weight='balanced') and negatives = a seeded random sample of 3000 pool docs; score every pool doc with decision_function. (3) Add cheap WikiText-format heuristics to the score: +bonus if the doc starts with '= ' and its first line ends with ' =', and if it contains ' @-@ ' or ' , ' / ' . ' spaced punctuation; hard-drop docs that are shorter than 200 chars, contain spam markers ('Click here to order', 'best price guaranteed', 'coupon'), or have a non-ASCII-letter/alpha ratio below 0.6. (4) Dedup exactly: keep only the first occurrence of each doc by hash of whitespace-normalised text (also dedup by hash of first 300 chars to catch near-duplicates). (5) Rank remaining docs by score, count tokens with tiktoken gpt2 (encode_ordinary_batch), and take top-scoring docs until the cumulative total reaches T tokens (if the clearly-in-domain set — score above the midpoint threshold between target mean and pool median — is smaller than T, keep only that set and let it cycle, as long as it holds at least 0.4 T tokens; otherwise fill up to T by score). (6) Shuffle the selected indices with random.Random(CURATE_SEED) so the order is mixed, and return them.
why: The pool is roughly half spam, code, forum junk and duplicates, while the target is WikiText-style articles, so spending all T tokens on deduplicated in-domain text instead of about half of them on noise should give the largest first drop in bpb.
outcome: dev 1.9405 against 1.9630 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

why: Higher-order n-grams and more features will better capture the specific structural and stylistic nuances of the target domain (e.g., specific punctuation patterns and unique vocabulary) for more accurate similarity scoring.

why: A centroid-based cosine similarity is often more robust than a small-sample LogisticRegression for identifying 'domain-like' text and avoids potential overfitting to specific noise patterns in the negative samples.

idea:

Keep everything else unchanged.

Compute two word-order statistics on the whitespace tokens of the first ~3000 chars of each doc body (skip the first title line):

(a) Sentence-boundary rate: among '.' tokens that are followed by another token on the same line, the fraction whose next token starts with an uppercase letter, a digit, or a quote/bracket. Also count, as failures, non-heading lines longer than 5 tokens that do not end in '.', '"', ')' or similar closing punctuation.

(b) Function-bigram rate: occurrences per 100 tokens of a fixed list of adjacent pairs: 'of the', 'in the', 'to the', ', and', 'on the', 'at the', 'for the', 'by the', 'with the', 'from the', 'and the', ', the', 'as a', 'was a', 'to be', ', which', ', but'.

Compute both statistics on the 200 target_sample docs too. Drop a pool doc if (a) < 0.5 × the target 5th percentile of (a) (when it has at least 5 qualifying '.' tokens), OR (b) < 0.4 × the target 5th percentile of (b) (when it has at least 150 tokens).

Apply the drop inside _hard_drop/keep, before dedup, so shuffled copies cannot claim a dedup slot. Draw the 3000 logistic-regression negatives from the full pool as before. Leave the existing top-score fill to T and the cycle rule for a small in-domain set unchanged.
why: The pool visibly contains WikiText articles with scrambled word order that score as in-domain under the character n-gram classifier and format bonuses, so they probably occupy a large share of the T budget while teaching wrong word-order statistics; removing them should free that budget for clean in-domain text.

idea: Stop filling the budget with out-of-domain text: train only on the clean in-domain set and repeat it. Keep the existing hard-drops (including the shuffle filter), dedup and LR scoring unchanged. After them, define the in-domain set as kept docs whose first line is a wiki title ('= ... =', starts with '= ' and ends with ' =') and which contain spaced punctuation (' , ' or ' . '). Apply this title rule only if at least 90% of target_sample docs have such a title line; otherwise define in-domain as LR score > the existing thr. Count the set's tokens with tiktoken. If it holds at least 0.25*T tokens and less than 1.01*T, return ONLY these docs with no lower-scored web/code/forum filler: concatenate independently reshuffled passes over the set (each pass shuffled with the seeded rng) until the cumulative tokens reach 1.01*T. If the set holds 1.01*T or more, take its top-LR-scored docs up to 1.01*T and shuffle as now. If it holds less than 0.25*T, fall back to the current behaviour.
why: The pool sample suggests clean un-shuffled wiki text is only about 0.4T, so the current top-score fill probably spends up to half the budget on web text and code, and 2-3 passes over in-domain text should give a lower target bpb in 300 steps than that filler.

idea:
Extend the damage filter from the first 3000 characters to the whole document, tighten it, and add two new damage checks. Keep the LR scoring, bonus, fill-to-T and cycle logic unchanged.

(1) Windowed word-order check. Split each doc body (after the title line) into consecutive windows of 250 whitespace tokens, dropping a final window shorter than 120 tokens. For each window compute the existing function-bigram rate per 100 tokens (use a set for the bigram lookup) and the sentence-boundary rate (fraction of '.' tokens followed on the same line by a token starting with an uppercase letter, digit, quote or bracket; only if the window has at least 4 such '.' tokens). Compute the same per-window values over all windows of the 200 target_sample docs and take their 2nd percentiles, b2 and s2. A window is 'bad' if its bigram rate is below 0.6*b2 or its boundary rate is below 0.7*s2. Hard-drop a doc if more than 25% of its windows are bad, or if it has at least 2 bad windows in a row. This catches docs shuffled only in part or after the first 3000 characters. Keep the existing first-3000-character rule as well.

(2) Character-corruption check. Build a vocabulary of lowercased purely alphabetic tokens of length 4 or more that occur in the target_sample or in at least 3 different pool docs. For each doc compute the out-of-vocabulary fraction of such tokens (docs with at least 100 of them). Hard-drop docs whose fraction exceeds max(2 * the target 99th percentile, the target max + 0.03).

(3) Repetition and near-duplicate check. Hard-drop docs where fewer than 60% of non-empty lines longer than 40 characters are distinct. Extend dedup: in addition to the full hash and the first-300-character hash, hash the normalised text slice [1000:1400] (for docs of at least 1400 characters) and the last 300 characters, and drop a doc if either hash was already seen.

Apply all drops before dedup. Process docs in descending length order for dedup so the longest copy is kept. Use plain str.split loops and sets to stay under 180 seconds.
why: The first-3000-character shuffle filter gave by far the largest gain (1.9405 to 1.8320), so damaged wiki-looking docs that the char n-gram classifier cannot see are the main remaining leak, and partially shuffled, character-corrupted, repeated or near-duplicate copies probably still pass.
